0-01.name: Knapped stone tools
0-01.hee1: If you hit a stone with another stone, it breaks and leaves an edge as sharp as a knife. Solid evidence goes back 2.6 million years (some say 3.3 million years ⚠️).

0-02.name: Fire making
0-02.hee1: Rub two pieces of wood together and they get hot, and at last a fire starts

0-03.name: Earthenware
0-03.hee1: Once clay is fired, water can never turn it back. People knew this 20,000 years ago.

0-04.name: Farming
0-04.hee1: Fields began when people kept choosing and growing wheat whose grains did not fall off easily.

0-05.name: Beans
0-05.hee1: Bean roots host bacteria that turn nitrogen from the air into fertilizer, so the field does not wear out easily.

0-06.name: Weaving
0-06.hee1: Soak flax stems in water until they rot, and you get fibers to spin into thread for cloth

0-07.name: Wool and the spindle whorl
0-07.hee1: A flywheel that spins like a top was used to twist wool into thread.

0-08.name: Woodworking
0-08.hee1: Grinding a stone axe gives it an edge that chips less easily.

0-09.name: Wheel
0-09.hee1: Before the wheel, there was the potter's wheel, a turning table for making pottery.

0-10.name: Lime burning
0-10.hee1: You can make it by burning seashells. It is the base of plaster for walls

0-11.name: Slaked lime and lime plaster
0-11.hee1: Slaked lime soaks up carbon dioxide from the air, turns back into stone, and hardens.

0-12.name: Charcoal
0-12.hee1: If you burn wood where there is little air, carbon-rich charcoal is left behind.

0-13.name: Cart
0-13.hee1: A four-wheeled cart pulled by oxen. People greased the axles with animal fat to make them slide.

0-14.name: Water transport
0-14.hee1: Heavy stones and ores are much easier to move floating on water than over land

0-15.name: Kiln
0-15.hee1: Surround a fire with walls and it gets hotter than an open-air fire. That heat made it possible to melt copper.

0-16.name: Salt pans
0-16.hee1: From nigari, the bittern used to set tofu, we can get magnesium metal for airplanes.

0-17.name: Domestication
0-17.hee1: The ancestor of cattle was the wild aurochs, nearly 2 m tall at the shoulder.

0-18.name: Rope
0-18.hee1: Even thin fibers can hold up heavy things once you twist them together (added in IMP-24, network_proposals N-2)

0-19.name: Potter's wheel
0-19.hee1: Before the wheel for carts, there was a spinning table for making pottery (the potter's wheel).

1-01.name: Germanium from coal ash
1-01.hee1: Germanium is sometimes concentrated in the ash left after burning coal.

1-02.name: Native copper
1-02.hee1: Some copper was found in the ground already as metal. Hammering makes it hard, and heating makes it soft again.

1-03.name: Copper smelting
1-03.hee1: Heat a green stone (malachite) with charcoal, and copper comes out

1-04.name: Copper smelting
1-04.hee1: Most copper today is taken from ores bonded with sulfur, by blowing air into them.

1-05.name: Bronze
1-05.hee1: Mix 10% tin into copper and you get bronze, which melts easily yet is hard.

1-06.name: Bloomery
1-06.hee1: Old furnaces could not melt iron, so it came out as a spongy lump.

1-07.name: Graphite
1-07.hee1: Graphite, the same stuff as pencil lead, was also used to make heat-proof crucibles

1-08.name: Wrought iron
1-08.hee1: Hammering red-hot iron squeezes out the slag mixed inside it.

1-09.name: Blast furnace
1-09.hee1: Make the furnace taller and blow air in harder, and the iron melts and flows out.

1-10.name: Coke blast furnace
1-10.hee1: When forests ran short of wood, people began making iron with coke, made by baking coal without air.

1-11.name: Crucible steel
1-11.hee1: Melt iron completely in a covered crucible and you get even, uniform steel. It was used for clock springs

1-12.name: Open-hearth furnace
1-12.hee1: A furnace that can melt scrap iron too, and slowly adjust what is in the steel.

1-13.name: Zinc
1-13.hee1: In an ordinary furnace zinc turns into a gas and escapes, so people cooled it to collect it.

1-14.name: Bayer process
1-14.hee1: Bauxite is dissolved in sodium hydroxide, the red iron-rich mud is filtered out, and alumina is taken out.

1-15.name: Metallurgical silicon
1-15.hee1: Silicon is made from "stone", "charcoal" and "lots of electricity"

1-16.name: Trichlorosilane synthesis and distillation
1-16.hee1: Silicon is first turned into a liquid that boils at 32°C, then cleaned by distillation.

1-17.name: Siemens process
1-17.hee1: A thin, hot silicon rod keeps getting thicker inside the gas.

1-18.name: Platinum refining
1-18.hee1: By pressing platinum powder together and hammering it, people got a metal they could work.

1-19.name: Rare earth separation
1-19.hee1: Rare earths are so alike that we separate them by using tiny differences, repeated hundreds of times

1-20.name: Platinum
1-20.hee1: Platinum is found as tiny bits of pure metal mixed in river sand.

1-21.name: Fluorite CaF2
1-21.hee1: Fluorite is found in ore veins together with galena and sphalerite.

1-22.name: Cassiterite SnO2
1-22.hee1: Tin ore is found near granite and in river sand.

1-23.name: Molybdenite MoS2
1-23.hee1: Molybdenum ore comes out as a side product of copper mines

1-24.name: Bauxite
1-24.hee1: Bauxite, the raw material for aluminum, is soil made when rocks weather in hot countries.

1-25.name: Monazite
1-25.hee1: Monazite is collected from sand together with iron sand.

1-26.name: Steel
1-26.hee1: 1) Just blowing air into iron turns it into steel. The color of the flame tells you when it is done. 2) Pig iron 4% -> steel 0.1-0.5%, with no fuel. 3) Bessemer 1856 and Kelly; steel became cheap, and rails and bridges became steel. 4) Mushet's spiegeleisen; the phosphorus problem -> Thomas 1878.

1-27.name: Lead
1-27.hee1: The metal of old water pipes and printing type. It is bad for your body

1-28.name: Tungsten wire
1-28.hee1: Its melting point is 3400°C, too high to melt, so the powder is pressed and baked solid.

1-29.name: Aluminium
1-29.hee1: Until then aluminium cost more than gold, and Napoleon III used it for tableware for his guests of honor.

1-30.name: Tin
1-30.hee1: A material for bronze 5,000 years ago becomes the light source of cutting-edge EUV.

1-31.name: Molybdenum smelting
1-31.hee1: The SO2 from roasting can be sent on as raw material for sulfuric acid [2-01]

1-32.name: Silver
1-32.hee1: The Iwami Silver Mine also got its silver by cupellation.

1-33.name: Boron
1-33.hee1: Borax has long been used as a "flux" for brazing metals.

1-34.name: Germanium tetrachloride distillation
1-34.hee1: Germanium is turned into a liquid that boils at 83°C, then purified by distillation.

1-35.name: Neodymium magnet
1-35.hee1: A magnet made of neodymium, iron and boron. It was born in Japan and the USA at almost the same time

1-36.name: Elemental boron
1-36.hee1: Magnesium steals the oxygen, leaving boron behind.

1-37.name: Nickel
1-37.hee1: Nickel becomes a gas with carbon monoxide, and when heated it turns back into pure nickel.

1-38.name: Synthetic cryolite
1-38.hee1: Natural cryolite was only found in Greenland, so today it is made by chemistry.

1-39.name: Magnesium
1-39.hee1: 1 L of seawater holds about 1.3 g of Mg. The Mg for aircraft in World War II was taken from the sea

1-40.name: Chromium
1-40.hee1: Thermite is still used today to weld railway rails on site.

1-41.name: Titanium
1-41.hee1: From the black grains mixed into iron sand, we get the metal used for airplane frames.

1-42.name: Lithium
1-42.hee1: Lithium is a metal so light it floats on water.

1-43.name: Antimony
1-43.hee1: Like water, antimony expands a little when it freezes (so the edges of printing type come out sharp)

1-44.name: Gallium
1-44.hee1: Gallium melts from the warmth of your palm (melting point about 30°C).

1-45.name: Mercury
1-45.hee1: It is what is inside a thermometer. Do not touch it.

1-46.name: Quartzite
1-46.hee1: A vein where white quartz filled a crack in the rock.

1-47.name: Lodestone
1-47.hee1: The first magnets were stones dug out of the ground

1-48.name: Basic oxygen furnace
1-48.hee1: Blow oxygen instead of air, and steel is made in a few tens of minutes. (Added in S-001. Sources: Wikipedia "Basic oxygen steelmaking", University of Leoben "70 Years of LD-Steelmaking")

1-49.name: Electric arc steelmaking
1-49.hee1: Old scrap iron is melted with electric sparks and made into new steel. (Added in S-001. Sources: Techniques de l'Ingénieur "History of the arc furnace", Wikipedia "Electric arc furnace")

1-50.name: Continuous casting
1-50.hee1: Steel keeps flowing without stopping, and a long slab is pulled out of the mold. (Added in S-001. Sources: encyclopedia.pub "Continuous casting", MDPI Metals review (continuous casting history, Junghans 1930s, CONCAST 1950s) (https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4701/12/5/862))

1-51.name: Rolling
1-51.hee1: Pass iron between two turning rollers and it quickly gets thinner and longer (added in S-001. Sources: Wikipedia "Rolling (metalworking)", ERIH "Henry Cort")

1-52.name: Extrusion
1-52.hee1: Push it out like squeezing toothpaste, and you get long aluminum bars all the same shape. (Added in S-001. Sources: Wikipedia "Extrusion", Grace's Guide "Extruded Metal Co")

1-53.name: Ferrite
1-53.hee1: The black magnets on your fridge are ferrite magnets, made like pottery. (Added in O-005. Sources: IEEE Milestones, Tokyo Institute of Technology "The invention of ferrite", Wikipedia "Ferrite (magnet)")

1-54.name: Invar
1-54.hee1: Just by mixing nickel into iron, you get a metal whose length hardly changes in summer or winter. (Added in O-005. Sources: Nobel Prize "Physics 1920", Nobel Prize "Physics 1920 Guillaume" (https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1920/guillaume/facts/))

1-55.name: Synthetic diamond
1-55.hee1: Most diamonds used in factories are synthetic diamonds made by squeezing graphite hard (added in O-010. Sources: ASME Landmark #198, Nobel Prize "Physics 1946", GIA, Wikipedia "Synthetic diamond")

1-56.name: Steam hammer
1-56.hee1: Huge blocks of steel that human arms cannot strike can be hit with 100 tons of force by a steam-powered hammer. (Added in O-010. Sources: ASME Landmark #69 "Creusot Steam Hammer", JSME "Mechanical Engineering Heritage No.058", Wikipedia "Steam hammer")

1-57.name: Carbon fiber
1-57.hee1: Carbon fiber weighs about a quarter as much as steel, yet is stronger than steel ⚠️ (Added in O-011. Sources: Wikipedia "National Historic Chemical Landmarks", Asia News Network)

1-58.name: Wire drawing
1-58.hee1: The copper wire in electric cables is made by pulling a thick rod through small holes dozens of times to stretch it thin. (Added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Wire drawing", ASME Landmark #139)

1-59.name: Puddling process
1-59.hee1: The iron of the Eiffel Tower is wrought iron, made by workers stirring the iron inside a furnace with a rod (added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Puddling (metallurgy)", "Henry Cort", Britannica "Puddling furnace", Grace's Guide "Henry Cort" (https://www.britannica.com/technology/puddling-furnace))

1-60.name: Electrolytic copper refining
1-60.hee1: The copper in electric wires is purified to 99.99% by electrolysis. (Added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Copper extraction", "James Balfour Elkington", OneMine (SME) 'Origins of Electrorefining: the World's First Commercial Electrorefinery' (https://www.onemine.org/documents/origins-of-electrorerefining-birth-of-the-technology-and-the-world-s-first-commercial-electrorefinery))

1-61.name: Thomas process
1-61.hee1: The phosphorus slag removed from iron became fertilizer for fields. (Added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Gilchrist–Thomas process" "Sidney Gilchrist Thomas", IOM3 "Steel heroes", Grace's Guide "Percy Gilchrist" (https://www.iom3.org/resource/steel-heroes.html))

1-62.name: Stainless steel
1-62.hee1: Stainless steel does not rust because an invisibly thin chromium film forms on the surface and protects it. (Added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Stainless steel", "Harry Brearley", Sheffield City Archives "Sources for the Study of Harry Brearley and Stainless Steel" (https://www.sheffield.gov.uk/sites/default/files/docs/libraries-and-archives/archives-and-local-studies/research/Stainless-Steel-and-Harry-Brearley-v-1-1--PDF--578-KB-.pdf))

1-63.name: Manganese addition
1-63.hee1: Adding just a little manganese made steel that used to crack easily strong (added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Robert Forester Mushet", "Mangalloy", Grace's Guide 'Robert Mushet' (https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/Robert_Mushet))

1-64.name: Gold extraction
1-64.hee1: One ton of gold ore often holds only a few grams of gold ⚠️ (Added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "MacArthur–Forrest process", "Patio process", Mining Foundation of the Southwest "Bartolomé de Medina" (https://miningfoundationsw.org/Bartolome_de_Medina))

1-65.name: High-speed steel
1-65.hee1: A high-speed steel blade stays sharp even when it gets hot enough to glow red. (Added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "High-speed steel" "Robert Forester Mushet", Knife Steel Nerds "The History of the First Tool Steel", West Yorkshire Steel "A History of High Speed Steel" (https://knifesteelnerds.com/2018/03/22/the-history-of-the-first-tool-steel/))

1-66.name: Tantalum
1-66.hee1: Light bulb filaments changed from carbon to tantalum to tungsten, each more heat-resistant than the last. (Added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Tantalum", "Werner von Bolton", Deutsche Biographie 'Bolton, Werner' (https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/sfz5200.html))

1-67.name: Froth flotation
1-67.hee1: The metal grains in ore stick to bubbles and float up (added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Froth flotation", Fuerstenau, Jameson, Yoon (eds.), Froth Flotation: A Century of Innovation (SME, 2007))

1-68.name: Permanent magnet steel
1-68.hee1: A magnet steel made by Japanese researchers was the strongest magnet in the world at the time. (Added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Kotaro Honda", Kotobank "MK steel", Japan Patent Office "Ten Great Japanese Inventors: Tokushichi Mishima")

1-69.name: Carburizing and nitriding
1-69.hee1: Only the surface of a gear is made hard, while the inside stays tough and hard to crack. (Added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Nitriding" "Carburizing", D. Pye, "Practical Nitriding and Ferritic Nitrocarburizing" (ASM International, 2003))

1-70.name: Zirconium and hafnium
1-70.hee1: Hafnium was only found after a method of studying elements with X-rays was developed. (Added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Hafnium", "Crystal bar process")

1-71.name: Heat treatment
1-71.hee1: The same steel can become totally different in hardness just by changing how fast you cool it (added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Quenching", "Isothermal transformation diagram", Davenport & Bain "Transformation of austenite at constant subcritical temperatures" Trans. AIME 90 (1930) (https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02643420))

1-72.name: Powder metallurgy and hot isostatic pressing
1-72.hee1: Metals that are very hard to melt are shaped by pressing powder and baking it. (Added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Powder metallurgy", "Hot isostatic pressing", ASME Landmark #103)

1-73.name: Coated steel sheet
1-73.hee1: The zinc on galvanized sheet rusts first itself, protecting the iron inside. (Added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Hot-dip galvanization" "Tinplate", 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica "Tin-plate and Terne-plate", Galvanizers Association "The potted history of galvanizing" (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Tin-plate_and_Terne-plate))

1-74.name: Cemented carbide
1-74.hee1: The cemented carbide name "Widia" means "like diamond" in German. (Added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Cemented carbide", "Tungsten carbide", Sandvik Coromant 'Celebrating 100 years of cemented carbide' / Mitsubishi Materials, history of cemented carbide (https://www.mmhm.co.jp/en/carbide/history.html))

1-75.name: Vacuum degassing
1-75.hee1: Suck molten steel up into a vacuum, and the gas hidden inside comes out as bubbles (added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Vacuum degassing", "Secondary steelmaking", AISE, The Making, Shaping and Treating of Steel (chapter on secondary refining))

1-76.name: Direct reduced iron
1-76.hee1: Make iron with hydrogen, and what comes out of the chimney is water, not carbon dioxide. (Added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Direct reduced iron", Midrex Technologies "It All Started in Portland… 50 Years Ago", VDEh "History of direct reduction" (https://www.midrex.com/tech-article/it-all-started-in-portland-50-years-ago/))

10-01.name: Electromagnet
10-01.hee1: A magnet that turns back into plain iron when you switch it off

10-02.name: Relay
10-02.hee1: A small clicking switch is the ancestor of the computer.

10-03.name: Telegraph
10-03.hee1: Thanks to the telegraph, news that took days by horse arrived in an instant.

10-04.name: Feedback control
10-04.hee1: Look at the gap from the target and correct it: that is the basis of all automatic control.

10-06.name: Relay computer
10-06.hee1: The first programmable computer was a bunch of clattering switches.

10-07.name: Vacuum tube flip-flops and computers
10-07.hee1: ENIAC's vacuum tubes burned out all the time, and they were replaced every day.

10-08.name: Magnetic-core memory
10-08.hee1: The memory of old computers was a hand-woven net of tiny magnets.

10-09.name: Transistor logic
10-09.hee1: Computers that filled a room shrank to about the size of a desk

10-10.name: IC logic
10-10.hee1: The computer that went to the Moon lined up thousands of small ICs, all the same kind.

10-11.name: Adders, counters and registers
10-11.hee1: Adding is just passing the "carry" to the next digit.

10-12.name: DRAM
10-12.hee1: Charge stored in a tiny capacitor is a "1". Left alone, it leaks away and is forgotten.

10-13.name: Microprocessor
10-13.hee1: The world's first microprocessor was born for a Japanese calculator

10-14.name: Microcomputer
10-14.hee1: Rice cookers and washing machines have small computers inside too.

10-15.name: Lithography machine control
10-15.hee1: The machines that make chips are run by those same chips.

10-16.name: Neural network
10-16.hee1: Starting from stones and sand, we arrived at a machine that can read numbers.

10-17.name: CAD
10-17.hee1: Keep drawings as numbers instead of on paper, and you can fix them as many times as you like (added in IMP-24, network_proposals N-7)

10-18.name: Compiler
10-18.hee1: "I want to give orders to a computer in human words" was the start of programming languages. (Added in IMP-24, network_proposals W-4)

10-19.name: VLSI design methodology
10-19.hee1: Even millions of transistors can be designed if you arrange them by fixed rules. (Added in IMP-24, network_proposals W-5)

10-20.name: Analytical Engine
10-20.hee1: In an age without electricity, a computer that ran programs with gears alone was designed. (Added in IMP-24, network_proposals N-8)

10-21.name: Slide rule
10-21.hee1: A ruler that turns multiplication into "adding lengths". Until calculators came, engineers always had one in their pocket (added in NET-06. Sources: Oughtred Society "History", Smithsonian "Slide Rules", Britannica "slide rule", ETHW "HP-35 Milestone")

10-22.name: Keyboard
10-22.hee1: Inside a keyboard is a small computer that checks which keys are pressed. (Added in S-002. Sources: Wikipedia "QWERTY", Computer Hope "Keyboard history")

10-23.name: Flash memory
10-23.hee1: Electrons are locked inside a thin glass wall, so it remembers for years even with the power off. (Added in S-002. Sources: Wikipedia "Fujio Masuoka" "Flash memory", Semiconductor History Museum of Japan (SSIS) "NAND flash memory")

10-24.name: SSD
10-24.hee1: The tiny computer inside an SSD quietly spreads out where it writes, so the same spot does not wear out from being written over and over. (Added in S-002. Sources: Computer History Museum "Solid State Drive Module Demonstrated", Wikipedia "Solid-state drive")

10-25.name: GPU
10-25.hee1: A GPU lines up thousands of small calculators that can only do simple math, and runs them all together (added in S-002. Sources: Wikipedia "GeForce 256", Jon Peddie Research "NEC µPD7220")

10-26.name: Industrial robot
10-26.hee1: The first robot to work in a factory took out hot metal parts that were dangerous for people to touch. (Added in S-005. Sources: The Henry Ford "Unimate", Guinness World Records "First industrial production robot", IEEE Spectrum)

10-27.name: Servomechanism
10-27.hee1: "Servo" comes from a French word meaning "to serve/obey," and at first it was the name of a device that turned a ship's rudder. (Added in S-005. Sources: Wikipedia "Joseph Farcot", Merriam-Webster "servomotor", Caltech "Harold Hazen")

10-28.name: Reinforcement learning
10-28.hee1: Without being taught the rules of a game, an AI got good just by watching the screen and the score and playing again and again. (Added in S-005. Sources: NSF "Barto and Sutton win 2024 Turing Award", Nature 518 (2015), Nature 529 (2016))

10-29.name: Transformer and large AI
10-29.hee1: The T in "GPT", often in the names of chat AIs, is the T of this Transformer (added in S-005. Sources: arXiv:1706.03762, Google Research "Attention Is All You Need")

10-30.name: SLAM (simultaneous localization and mapping)
10-30.hee1: A robot vacuum guesses "Where am I?" and "What shape is the room?" bit by bit, with the same calculation. (Added in S-004. Sources: doc.ic.ac.uk, arxiv.org)

10-31.name: Stored-program computer
10-31.hee1: The first stored-program computer remembered numbers as dots on a CRT screen, like a TV. (Added in O-008. Sources: IEEE Milestones "Manchester University Baby Computer 1948-1951", Wikipedia "Turing Award")

10-32.name: Floating-point standard
10-32.hee1: When a computer calculates 0.1 + 0.2, the answer can be just slightly off from 0.3. (Added in O-010. Sources: IEEE Milestones "IEEE Standard 754, 1985", "Intel 8087, 1980", IEEE Milestone "IEEE Standard 754 for Binary Floating-Point Arithmetic, 1985" (https://ethw.org/Milestones:IEEE_Standard_754_for_Binary_Floating-Point_Arithmetic,_1985))

10-33.name: Hard disk drive
10-33.hee1: The first hard disk stacked 50 platters about 60 cm across, and held only about 5 MB (added in O-011. Sources: ASME Landmark #90 "IBM 350 RAMAC", Wikipedia "IBM 350", National Museum of Nature and Science "Essential Historical Materials for Science and Technology")

10-34.name: Operating system
10-34.hee1: The ideas of UNIX from more than 50 years ago still live inside smartphones. (Added in O-011. Sources: Wikipedia "Turing Award", "Compatible Time-Sharing System", "Unix", IEEE Computer Society 'Fernando Jose Corbató' / MIT CSAIL (https://history.computer.org/pioneers/corbato.html))

10-35.name: Circuit simulator
10-35.hee1: Before chips are made, they are run many times inside a computer to check them. (Added in O-011. Sources: IEEE Milestones "SPICE, 1969-1970", IEEE Milestone "SPICE, 1969-1970" (ETHW) (https://ethw.org/Milestones:SPICE_Circuit_Simulation_Program))

10-36.name: RISC
10-36.hee1: Smartphone CPUs are descendants of a design that made instructions simple on purpose to make them faster. (Added in O-011. Sources: IEEE Milestones "RISC-I", Wikipedia "Reduced instruction set computer")

10-37.name: Predicting protein shapes with AI
10-37.hee1: AI can now guess how a protein folds just from its order of amino acids (added in O-011. Sources: Nobel Prize "Chemistry 2024", "Chemistry 1972", Nobel Prize "The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2024 press release" (https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2024/press-release/))

11-01.name: Irrigation
11-01.hee1: Too much watering ruins a field with salt.

11-02.name: Plow
11-02.hee1: The steel plow turned the great prairies of North America into farmland.

11-03.name: Crop rotation
11-03.hee1: Growing beans makes the field richer.

11-04.name: Plant breeding
11-04.hee1: Genetics began with peas in a monastery garden

11-05.name: Compost
11-05.hee1: Tiny creatures that eat fallen leaves make fertilizer.

11-06.name: Superphosphate
11-06.hee1: Dissolve bones in sulfuric acid and they become fertilizer.

11-07.name: Nitrogen fertilizer
11-07.hee1: Nitrogen from the air becomes bread.

11-08.name: Milling
11-08.hee1: Grinding flour was one of the first jobs people gave to machines

11-09.name: Bread
11-09.hee1: The holes in bread are yeast farts (CO2).

11-10.name: Alcohol and vinegar
11-10.hee1: Leave alcohol out in the air and it turns into vinegar.

11-11.name: Salting, drying and smoking
11-11.hee1: Salt was once called "white gold", and it is said to be the origin of the word salary ⚠️.

11-12.name: Canning
11-12.hee1: For about 50 years after cans were invented, there was no can opener⚠️

11-13.name: Refrigeration and freezing
11-13.hee1: The refrigerator and liquid air were made by the same person.

11-14.name: Sugar
11-14.hee1: White sugar is brown juice that was whitened with charcoal.

11-15.name: Pasteurization
11-15.hee1: The word "pasteurized" on milk cartons comes from Pasteur's name.

11-16.name: Bordeaux mixture
11-16.hee1: A blue spray put on roadside grapes to stop theft turned out to prevent disease

11-17.name: Espresso pressure brewing
11-17.hee1: Espresso is made by forcing hot water through coffee grounds at about 9 atmospheres, roughly 4 times the air pressure in a tire. (Added in S-004. Sources: en.wikipedia.org, gaggia.com, home-barista.com)

12-01.name: Roman concrete
12-01.hee1: Roman concrete from 2000 years ago actually gets stronger in seawater ⚠️

12-02.name: Portland cement
12-02.hee1: It got its name because its color looked like the stone from the Isle of Portland.

12-03.name: Reinforced concrete
12-03.hee1: Reinforced concrete was born from flower pots

12-04.name: Steel frame construction
12-04.hee1: The Eiffel Tower's height changes by more than ten centimeters between summer and winter.

12-05.name: Flat glass
12-05.hee1: Window glass is made by "floating it on melted metal."

12-06.name: Water supply
12-06.hee1: Microbes living in a layer of sand clean the water.

12-07.name: Chlorination
12-07.hee1: The smell of a swimming pool is the smell of chlorine that prevents disease

12-08.name: Sewer system
12-08.hee1: It started because the smell got so bad that Parliament could not meet.

12-09.name: Roads
12-09.hee1: "Tarmac" comes from coal tar and Mr. McAdam's name.

12-10.name: Bridge
12-10.hee1: A framework of triangles (a truss) does not lose its shape.

12-11.name: Surveying
12-11.hee1: Tadataka Ino measured all of Japan by his steps

12-12.name: Ventilation and air conditioning
12-12.hee1: Air conditioning was born not for people, but for paper.

12-13.name: HEPA filter
12-13.hee1: The hardest particle size to catch is 0.3 µm.

12-14.name: Laminar-flow cleanroom
12-14.hee1: Chips are made in rooms thousands of times cleaner than an operating room.

12-15.name: Lightning rod
12-15.hee1: Minecraft's lightning rod is made of copper, just like the real thing

12-16.name: Elevator safety brake
12-16.hee1: Otis did not invent the elevator; what he made was a catch that stops it from falling even if the rope breaks. (Added in S-004. Sources: asme.org, theelevatormuseum.org, invent.org)

12-17.name: Electric elevator and counterweight
12-17.hee1: On the other end of an elevator's rope hangs a weight about as heavy as the car, so the motor only lifts the "difference in weight." (Added in S-004. Sources: en.wikipedia.org, theelevatormuseum.org, britannica.com)

13-01.name: Soap and handwashing
13-01.hee1: The doctor who told people to wash their hands was laughed at while he was alive.

13-02.name: Antisepsis
13-02.hee1: The mouthwash Listerine is named after Lister

13-03.name: Anesthesia
13-03.hee1: The world's first surgery under general anesthesia was done in Japan.

13-04.name: Bacteriology
13-04.hee1: Diseases were spread by living things too small to see.

13-05.name: Agar medium
13-05.hee1: Research on bacteria moved forward thanks to a kitchen trick from jam making.

13-06.name: Vaccine
13-06.hee1: The word vaccine comes from the Latin word for "cow"

13-07.name: Epidemiology
13-07.hee1: Just putting dots on a map revealed the cause of a disease.

13-08.name: Aspirin
13-08.hee1: How the medicine works was found out more than 70 years after it went on sale.

13-09.name: Sulfa drugs
13-09.hee1: The first antibacterial drug was a dye for coloring cloth.

13-10.name: Penicillin
13-10.hee1: The mold used for mass production was found on a rotten melon from a market

13-11.name: X-ray diagnosis
13-11.hee1: Röntgen did not patent it, so that anyone could use it.

13-12.name: Blood transfusion and blood types
13-12.hee1: Until blood types were known, a transfusion was a gamble.

13-13.name: Thermometer
13-13.hee1: Old thermometers were as long as 30 cm.

13-14.name: Fluoride and teeth
13-14.hee1: The fluorine in toothpaste is the same element as the fluorine in excimer lasers

13-15.name: Medical oxygen
13-15.hee1: Hospital oxygen is taken from air turned into liquid.

14-01.name: Canals and locks
14-01.hee1: On a canal's staircase, ships climb mountains.

14-02.name: Compass
14-02.hee1: A compass needle moves because the Earth itself is a giant magnet.

14-03.name: Longitude and the chronometer
14-03.hee1: How accurate a clock was decided where a ship was

14-04.name: Steamship
14-04.hee1: Ships that could move without wind made the world smaller.

14-05.name: Railways
14-05.hee1: The width of railway tracks is said to come from the wheel spacing of horse carts ⚠️

14-06.name: Steel rails
14-06.hee1: Steel rails lasted more than 10 times longer than iron rails ⚠️.

14-07.name: Pneumatic tire
14-07.hee1: The pneumatic tire was made by a veterinarian for his child

14-08.name: Bicycle
14-08.hee1: The first bicycles had no pedals.

14-09.name: Internal combustion engine
14-09.hee1: An engine's four beats are "suck, squeeze, bang, blow."

14-10.name: Diesel engine
14-10.hee1: A diesel engine ran on peanut oil.

14-11.name: Automobile
14-11.hee1: The first long-distance drive was a wife's trip with her children, kept secret from her husband

14-12.name: Airplane
14-12.hee1: The Wright brothers ran a bicycle shop.

14-13.name: Duralumin
14-13.hee1: Left alone over a weekend, the metal had hardened all by itself.

14-14.name: Electric railway
14-14.hee1: Subways were only possible with smoke-free electricity.

14-15.name: Rocket equation
14-15.hee1: Even in space, with no air to push on, a rocket moves by the recoil of its own exhaust (IMP-24: changed from "Rocket" to "Rocket equation" in T-3)

14-16.name: Self-driving cars
14-16.hee1: In the first driverless car race, not a single car finished; even the one that went farthest covered only about 1/20 of the course. (Added in S-005. Sources: AI Magazine (2009) Urmson et al., DTIC "DARPA Grand Challenge")

14-17.name: Air brake
14-17.hee1: The air brake is built to "stop when the air leaks out," so even when it breaks it fails on the safe side. (Added in S-004. Sources: en.wikipedia.org, britannica.com)

14-18.name: Drum brakes and disc brakes
14-18.hee1: Brakes stop a car by turning its motion into "heat", so they can get too hot going down a mountain road. (Added in S-004. Sources: en.wikipedia.org, classicsworld.co.uk)

14-19.name: Automatic transmission
14-19.hee1: The first mass-produced automatic transmission shifted gears by "oil pressure", not by working pedals. (added in S-004. Sources: en.wikipedia.org, ateupwithmotor.com)

14-20.name: Turbocharger
14-20.hee1: A turbo uses the force of exhaust gas, which would be wasted, to push air into the engine. (Added in S-004. Sources: en.wikipedia.org, accelleron-industries.com)

15-01.name: Paper
15-01.hee1: Paper used to be made from rags; today it is made from wood.

15-02.name: Movable-type printing
15-02.hee1: Type metal is a rare alloy that expands when it hardens.

15-03.name: Submarine cable
15-03.hee1: The cable's insulation was rubber made from tree sap

15-04.name: Telephone
15-04.hee1: Telephone microphones were made of carbon grains.

15-05.name: Phonograph
15-05.hee1: The first words ever recorded were "Mary Had a Little Lamb."

15-06.name: Discovery of radio waves
15-06.hee1: Hertz said, "This discovery is of no use at all" ⚠️.

15-07.name: Wireless telegraphy
15-07.hee1: In the Titanic disaster, some people were rescued in time thanks to radio

15-08.name: Crystal radio
15-08.hee1: The point-contact transistor's "needle standing on a crystal" is a descendant of the crystal radio.

15-09.name: Vacuum tube radio
15-09.hee1: At first, radios were as big as furniture.

15-10.name: Transistor radio
15-10.hee1: In 1954, a radio using transistors went on sale.

15-11.name: Television
15-11.hee1: The first image on Japanese television was the katakana letter "イ" (i)

15-12.name: Magnetic recording
15-12.hee1: The brown on cassette tape is rusted iron powder.

15-13.name: Optical fiber
15-13.hee1: Light cables running along the sea floor carry the world's internet.

15-14.name: Information theory
15-14.hee1: The word "bit" spread through Shannon's paper.

15-15.name: Computer networks
15-15.hee1: The first network message stopped after 2 letters, "LO" (it crashed partway through LOGIN)

15-16.name: USB
15-16.hee1: Before USB, computers had several differently shaped ports: one for the mouse, one for the keyboard, one for the printer. (Added in S-002. Sources: IEEE Milestones "Universal Serial Bus (USB)", heise "30 years of USB 1.0")

15-17.name: Wi-Fi
15-17.hee1: "Wi-Fi" does not stand for anything; it is a name chosen to be easy to remember. (Added in S-002. Sources: Wikipedia "Wi-Fi Alliance", EE World "Wi-Fi's long road")

15-18.name: Capacitive touchscreen
15-18.hee1: Just by bringing your finger close, invisible electrodes under the screen notice "there is a finger here". (Added in S-003. Sources: Electronics Letters (1965), CERN "The first touchscreens", Google Patents US3482241)

15-19.name: Loudspeaker
15-19.hee1: A loudspeaker makes sound by shaking paper with a magnet and a coil of wire (a cousin of the motor) (added in S-003. Sources: Wikipedia "Loudspeaker", Britannica "Loudspeaker", Trans. AIEE (1925))

15-20.name: Mobile phone radio
15-20.hee1: The world's first mobile phone network was the car phone in Tokyo in 1979. (Added in S-003. Sources: Wikipedia "History of mobile phones", Britannica "Mobile telephone", NTT Docomo "History")

15-21.name: Bluetooth
15-21.hee1: Bluetooth is named after the nickname "Blue Tooth" of an old king who united countries. (Added in S-003. Sources: Bluetooth SIG "Origin of the Bluetooth name", Ericsson "Bluetooth: a wireless success story")

15-22.name: Antenna
15-22.hee1: An antenna's length is set by the wavelength of the radio waves it receives. For smartphone Wi-Fi, it is about 3 cm. (Added in S-003. Sources: Wikipedia "Antenna (radio)", "Inverted-F antenna", Britannica "Antenna")

15-23.name: Condenser microphone
15-23.hee1: Studio microphones catch sound with the gap between a very thin film that moves with sound and a plate (added in S-004. Sources: mmrmagazine.com, dpamicrophones.com)

15-24.name: Dynamic microphone
15-24.hee1: A karaoke microphone works the same way as a speaker used in reverse. (Added in S-004. Sources: mixonline.com, en.wikipedia.org)

15-25.name: Electret condenser microphone
15-25.hee1: Many microphones in phones and toys are made of a plastic film that keeps an electric charge stored in it. (Added in S-004. Sources: aps.org, lemelson.mit.edu)

15-26.name: MEMS microphone
15-26.hee1: A smartphone has several tiny microphones carved from silicon, and they are also used to cancel noise. (Added in S-004. Sources: businesswirechina.com, nt.tu-darmstadt.de)

15-27.name: Yagi-Uda antenna
15-27.hee1: The rods lined up on a rooftop TV antenna are shaped to gather radio waves from one direction (added in O-010. Sources: IEEE Milestones "Directive Short Wave Antenna, 1924", ETHW "Yagi Antenna", Wikipedia "Yagi–Uda antenna")

15-28.name: Optical disc
15-28.hee1: A scratched CD still plays because the broken parts are fixed by calculation. (Added in O-010. Sources: Wikipedia "Compact disc", National Museum of Nature and Science "Essential Historical Materials for Science and Technology")

15-29.name: Error-correcting code
15-29.hee1: QR codes hide extra information so they can still be read when a little dirty or chipped. (Added in O-011. Sources: IEEE Computer Society "Richard Hamming", Wikipedia "Hamming code")

15-30.name: Public-key cryptography
15-30.hee1: You can shop online because of the math of a "lock" that anyone can close but only you can open. (Added in O-011. Sources: Wikipedia "Turing Award", "Public-key cryptography", ACM A.M. Turing Award 2015 (public-key cryptography, 1976) (https://amturing.acm.org/award_winners/diffie_8371646.cfm))

15-31.name: Rotary-head videotape
15-31.hee1: Videotape had a small head spinning faster than the tape, writing the picture at a slant (added in O-011. Sources: Wikipedia "Videotape", "VHS", National Museum of Nature and Science "Essential Historical Materials for Science and Technology")

2-01.name: Sulfuric acid
2-01.hee1: Join oxygen to sulfur dioxide and let water absorb it, and you get sulfuric acid.

2-02.name: Potash
2-02.hee1: The name potassium comes from "pot ash", the ash left in a pot.

2-03.name: Natural soda
2-03.hee1: A salt that was even used to make mummies in ancient Egypt

2-04.name: Kelp ash soda
2-04.hee1: Soda was obtained from seaweed ash, and iodine was discovered in the liquid from that ash.

2-05.name: Leblanc process
2-05.hee1: A way to make soda from salt and sulfuric acid. The hydrochloric acid gas it gave off was at first just released into the sky.

2-06.name: Solvay process
2-06.hee1: Soda is made from salt, ammonia and carbon dioxide. The ammonia is recovered and used again.

2-07.name: Potassium dichromate
2-07.hee1: The name chromium comes from the Greek word for "color", because it makes compounds of many colors

2-08.name: Caustic soda
2-08.hee1: Mix soda with slaked lime and you get caustic soda.

2-09.name: Soap
2-09.hee1: Mix oil with a strong alkali and you get soap.

2-10.name: Hydrofluoric acid
2-10.hee1: Hydrofluoric acid dissolves glass, so it cannot be kept in a glass bottle.

2-11.name: Hydrogen sulfide and sulfur recovery
2-11.hee1: Sulfur was won back from the waste of soda factories

2-12.name: Sulfates
2-12.hee1: Pass electricity through copper sulfate solution, and copper sticks to a mold in its shape.

2-13.name: Lime cycle and calcium chloride
2-13.hee1: Lime is burned, splashed with water, and turns back into stone in the air. It can be used round and round.

2-14.name: Soda-lime glass
2-14.hee1: Sand alone needs 1700°C, but with soda mixed in it melts at 1000°C.

2-15.name: Borosilicate glass
2-15.hee1: Science-room beakers don't crack over a flame thanks to boron

2-16.name: Distilled water
2-16.hee1: Boil water and cool the steam, and you get water with no salt left in it.

2-17.name: Ion exchange
2-17.hee1: A relative of Bakelite cleans water.

2-18.name: Ultrapure water
2-18.hee1: Ultrapure water conducts electricity only as much as water itself splits into a tiny amount of ions.

2-19.name: Hydrogen peroxide
2-19.hee1: Hydrogen peroxide later became possible to make by electrolysis too

2-20.name: Coal tar
2-20.hee1: Bake coal without air, and you get coke, gas, and black tar.

2-21.name: Ammonia water
2-21.hee1: Ammonia used to be a side product of gasworks.

2-22.name: Aqua regia
2-22.hee1: In 1940, to protect them from the Nazis, Hevesy dissolved the Nobel Prize medals of Laue and Franck in aqua regia and left them on a shelf. After the war, the gold was recovered and the medals were made again.

2-23.name: Wood distillation
2-23.hee1: Neanderthals made tar from birch bark about 200,000 years ago (Campitello)

2-24.name: Benzene
2-24.hee1: In 1856 Perkin made mauve (the first synthetic dye) from tar, and the chemical industry began (candidate branch [B-xx]).

2-25.name: Phenol
2-25.hee1: Phenol, found in coal tar, was used to disinfect during surgery.

2-26.name: Methanol
2-26.hee1: Distilling the liquid from burnt wood gives methanol (wood spirit).

2-27.name: Formaldehyde
2-27.hee1: Methanol is reacted with oxygen over a hot copper or silver mesh

2-28.name: Phenolic resin
2-28.hee1: The first synthetic plastic was made from phenol and formaldehyde.

2-29.name: Rubber
2-29.hee1: Add sulfur to rubber and heat it, and it becomes strong rubber that does not get sticky even when hot.

2-30.name: Negative photoresist
2-30.hee1: A material that hardens only where light hits it. It was used to copy IC patterns.

2-31.name: Films that harden in light: asphalt and dichromated gelatin
2-31.hee1: The first photograph and the way ICs are made use the same principle

2-32.name: Positive photoresist
2-32.hee1: A material that dissolves only where light hits it. It was first invented for paper used to copy drawings.

2-33.name: Chemically amplified resist
2-33.hee1: One acid made by light sets off hundreds of reactions. That is why a pattern can be copied with very little light.

2-35.name: Crude oil and distillation
2-35.hee1: Crude oil is heated and separated into gas, kerosene, heavy oil and more by their different boiling temperatures.

2-36.name: Ethylene
2-36.hee1: Take water out of alcohol and it becomes a gas called ethylene

2-37.name: Polyethylene
2-37.hee1: Polyethylene was discovered by accident in an experiment using very high pressure.

2-38.name: PTFE
2-38.hee1: It was used in the Manhattan Project to handle UF6 (a corrosive gas).

2-39.name: Ethanol
2-39.hee1: Yeast is what makes alcoholic drinks. But even by distilling, you cannot get it stronger than 95.6%.

2-40.name: Acetone
2-40.hee1: Weizmann later became the first president of Israel

2-41.name: Epoxy resin
2-41.hee1: The glue that hardens when you mix two tubes together is epoxy.

2-42.name: Acetic acid
2-42.hee1: Pure acetic acid freezes like ice in a slightly cold room.

2-43.name: Oil of vitriol
2-43.hee1: Long ago, sulfuric acid was an "oil" made by roasting green crystals.

2-44.name: Red phosphorus
2-44.hee1: The striking surface of a matchbox is coated with red phosphorus

2-45.name: Light-curing resin
2-45.hee1: The resin used to draw chip circuits and the resin in 3D printers work the same way. (Added in IMP-24, network_proposals N-6)

2-46.name: Transparent electrode ITO
2-46.hee1: Indium is named after the indigo color seen when the light of its flame was split. (Added in S-003. Sources: RSC "Indium", USGS "Mineral Commodity Summaries 2024: Indium", Wikipedia "Indium tin oxide")

2-47.name: Chemically strengthened glass
2-47.hee1: Pushing big atoms into small gaps squeezes the glass surface tight and makes it harder to break. (Added in S-003. Sources: Corning "Innovations", WIRED "The Glass That Saved Corning", Wikipedia "Chemically strengthened glass")

2-48.name: CFC refrigerants
2-48.hee1: CFCs were made as safe, non-toxic refrigerants, yet high in the sky they were destroying the ozone layer (added in S-004. Sources: en.wikipedia.org, inventionandtech.com)

2-49.name: Polyurethane foam insulation
2-49.hee1: Inside a refrigerator's walls is plastic packed with tiny bubbles. (Added in S-004. Sources: en.wikipedia.org, plasticstoday.com)

2-50.name: Coordination polymerization catalyst
2-50.hee1: The plastic in bottle caps is made by joining molecules one by one on a metal catalyst. (Added in O-008. Sources: Nobel Prize "Chemistry 1963", ACS "Polypropylene and High-Density Polyethylene")

2-51.name: Nylon
2-51.hee1: On the day nylon stockings went on sale, thousands of people lined up at the stores. (Added in O-010. Sources: Wikipedia "National Historic Chemical Landmarks", ACS "Landmarks directory")

2-52.name: Boranes
2-52.hee1: Diborane catches fire just by touching air, so chemists long ago built their own air-free apparatus (added in O-011. Sources: Nobel Prize "Chemistry 1976", Lipscomb Nobel Lecture 1976 (nobelprize.org) (https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/lipscomb-lecture.pdf))

2-53.name: Catalytic cracking
2-53.hee1: Much of the gasoline in cars is made by breaking heavy crude oil apart over a catalyst. (Added in O-011. Sources: Wikipedia "National Historic Chemical Landmarks", ACS "Landmarks directory")

2-54.name: Chromatography
2-54.hee1: The name chromatography means "color writing." At first it separated plant pigments into bands of color. (Added in O-011. Sources: Nobel Prize "Chemistry 1952", Wikipedia "National Historic Chemical Landmarks")

2-55.name: Conductive polymers
2-55.hee1: Plastic that conducts electricity was born from a mistake in the amount of material used in an experiment. (Added in O-011. Sources: Nobel Prize "Chemistry 2000", WIPO Magazine 2020)

2-56.name: Automatic glass-forming machines
2-56.hee1: Glass bulbs for light bulbs came to be blown by machine, hundreds per minute (added in O-011. Sources: ASME Landmark #86 "Owens AR Bottle Machine", #81 "Corning Ribbon Machine", ASME Landmark #81 "Corning Ribbon Machine" (up to about 2000 per minute) (https://www.asme.org/about-asme/engineering-history/landmarks/81-corning-ribbon-machine))

2-57.name: Diazonaphthoquinone
2-57.hee1: A powder that breaks down when light hits it became the "eye" that copies IC patterns.

3-01.name: Campfire
3-01.hee1: The heat of a campfire escapes into the surroundings.

3-02.name: Hearth stove
3-02.hee1: When you surround a fire with walls, the heat bounces back off them, making it hotter than a campfire.

3-04.name: Bellows
3-04.hee1: Blowing air makes a fire hotter. The name of Japan's tatara furnace comes from this bellows

3-05.name: Blast furnace
3-05.hee1: In a tall furnace that burns coke with a strong blast of air, iron flows out as a liquid.

3-06.name: Reverberatory furnace
3-06.hee1: When ore is roasted, sulfur leaves as smoke. It used to be poisonous smoke, but if collected it becomes sulfuric acid.

3-07.name: Crucible furnace
3-07.hee1: Melting things in a crucible keeps the fuel and flame from dirtying what is inside.

3-08.name: Converter (Bessemer process)
3-08.hee1: Just blowing air into molten iron raises its temperature, with no fuel

3-09.name: Thermocouple
3-09.hee1: Before that, in 1782 Wedgwood measured kiln temperature by how much clay shrank.

3-10.name: Acheson furnace
3-10.hee1: Heat carbon with electricity way too much and it becomes graphite.

3-11.name: Optical pyrometer
3-11.hee1: It measures temperature by comparing the color of a hot object with the color of a light bulb filament.

3-12.name: Firebrick
3-12.hee1: Ordinary bricks melt in a furnace. Only bricks rich in quartz can stand it

3-13.name: Thermal insulation
3-13.hee1: Diatomaceous earth is soil full of gaps, made from piled-up shells of tiny living things.

3-14.name: Induction furnace
3-14.hee1: Same principle as an induction (IH) cooktop. CHEMISTRY #142

3-15.name: Arc furnace
3-15.hee1: An electric spark (arc) makes heat of over 2000°C.

3-16.name: Vacuum furnace
3-16.hee1: Heat things after pumping out the air, and they bake without rusting

3-18.name: Regenerative furnace (equipment)
3-18.hee1: A furnace that uses the heat of exhaust gas, which would be wasted, to warm up the next air.

3-19.name: By-product coke oven
3-19.hee1: Old coke ovens burned off and threw away their gas and tar.

3-20.name: Fireclay
3-20.hee1: Since ancient times, crucibles and furnace linings have been made of heat-resistant clay.

3-21.name: Heat pipe
3-21.hee1: Inside is a vacuum with only a little water, so the water boils even at about body temperature and carries heat (added in S-002. Sources: Wikipedia "Heat pipe", C&R Technologies "Two-Phase Musing")

3-22.name: Vapor-compression refrigeration cycle
3-22.hee1: A refrigerator is not a machine that makes cold; it is a "heat pump" that pumps the heat inside out. (Added in S-004. Sources: asme.org, en.wikipedia.org)

3-23.name: Heat pump
3-23.hee1: An air conditioner's heating gathers heat even from the cold outside air in winter and carries it into the room. (Added in S-004. Sources: en.wikipedia.org, austria-forum.org)

3-24.name: Heating wire heater
3-24.hee1: The glowing red wires in a toaster are made of a special metal mixing nickel and chromium, so they do not burn out even when red hot. (Added in S-004. Sources: en.wikipedia.org, en.wikipedia.org, hagley.org)

4-01.name: Water-wheel generator
4-01.hee1: The more water flows and the higher it falls, the more electricity you can make

4-02.name: Steam engine
4-02.hee1: The first steam engines were for pumping water out of coal mines.

4-03.name: Copper cable
4-03.hee1: Some of the electricity flowing through a wire is lost as heat. Thick wires and high voltage reduce the loss.

4-04.name: Dynamo and natural magnets
4-04.hee1: Spinning a coil near a magnet makes electricity.

4-05.name: Self-excited dynamo
4-05.hee1: It can make electricity without a magnet

4-06.name: Steam turbine
4-06.hee1: Steam spins a bladed wheel fast. Because it spins so fast, it is the best fit for making electricity.

4-07.name: Lead-acid battery
4-07.hee1: The same as a car battery.

4-08.name: Electric motor
4-08.hee1: A motor is the opposite of a generator. Send electricity through it and it spins.

4-09.name: High-frequency oscillator
4-09.hee1: The machines that made transistors ran on vacuum tubes

4-10.name: Transformer
4-10.hee1: With alternating current, you can raise or lower the voltage. Sending power at high voltage loses less electricity.

4-11.name: Rectifier
4-11.hee1: It turns AC into DC. Electrolysis needs DC.

4-12.name: Electric furnace
4-12.hee1: Even without nichrome, you can make a heating element from a graphite rod.

4-13.name: Voltaic pile
4-13.hee1: The first battery was a stack of copper and zinc disks with cloth soaked in salt water between them

4-14.name: Steam power generation
4-14.hee1: In 1882, electricity made with steam lit up a city for the first time.

4-15.name: Lithium-ion battery
4-15.hee1: Charging means tucking lithium ions into the gaps in graphite. (Added in IMP-24, network_proposals N-3)

4-16.name: Arc lamp
4-16.hee1: Electric light began with "sparks", before the light bulb. (Added in IMP-24, network_proposals N-9)

4-17.name: Stepper motor
4-17.hee1: Each time you send a pulse of electricity, it turns by exactly a set angle, click (added in S-001. Sources: Nidec "History of the Motor", Wikipedia "Marius Lavet")

4-18.name: Electric fan
4-18.hee1: The first electric fan was just a motor with a propeller on it. (Added in S-002. Sources: Wikipedia "Schuyler Wheeler", ETHW "Schuyler Wheeler")

4-19.name: Switching power supply
4-19.hee1: Phone chargers are small because they switch the electricity on and off tens of thousands of times a second, which lets the transformer be small. (Added in S-002. Sources: righto.com "Apple didn't revolutionize power supplies", Wikipedia "Switched-mode power supply")

4-20.name: Vibration motor
4-20.hee1: The weight is attached on only one side, so when it spins the whole device shakes. (Added in S-003. Sources: Google Patents US4794392, Wikipedia "Vibrating alert")

4-21.name: Brushless DC motor
4-21.hee1: The motors in computer fans and air conditioners have no parts that rub and wear out (added in S-004. Sources: en.wikipedia.org, technav.ieee.org)

4-22.name: Induction motor
4-22.hee1: No wires are connected to the spinning part of an induction motor, yet it turns, pulled by an invisible "rotating magnet". (Added in S-004. Sources: ethw.org, en.wikipedia.org, patents.google.com)

4-23.name: Cross-flow fan
4-23.hee1: Inside an air conditioner's indoor unit is a long, thin impeller shaped like a chikuwa tube, which blows a wide sheet of air. (Added in S-004. Sources: patents.google.com, research.unipd.it)

4-24.name: Bladeless fan
4-24.hee1: A bladeless fan actually has blades inside its base, and the air coming out of the ring pulls the surrounding air along, multiplying the flow many times. (Added in S-004. Sources: designingbuildings.co.uk, arxiv.org)

4-25.name: Regenerative braking
4-25.hee1: When an electric car brakes, it can recharge its battery a little with the electricity made at that moment. (added in S-004. Sources: en.wikipedia.org, en.wikipedia.org, Science Museum Group "Electric brougham motor car (Kriéger, 1904)", Grace's Guide "J. S. Raworth" (https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/objects/co8038670/electric-brougham-motor-car-electric))

4-26.name: EV fast charging
4-26.hee1: In fast charging, the charger and the car talk to each other and decide "this much current right now". (Added in S-004. Sources: en.wikipedia.org, www4.tepco.co.jp)

4-27.name: Induction coil
4-27.hee1: From a single battery it can make lightning-like sparks of tens of thousands of volts. (Added in O-006. Sources: IEEE Milestones "Callan's Pioneering Contributions 1836", Wikipedia "Induction coil")

4-28.name: Dry cell battery
4-28.hee1: Even a "dry" cell is not completely dry inside; it holds a damp paste. (Added in O-009. Sources: ACS "Columbia Dry Cell Battery", ACS "Columbia Dry Cell Battery" (chemical landmark) (https://www.acs.org/education/whatischemistry/landmarks/drycellbattery.html))

4-29.name: Gas turbines and jet engines
4-29.hee1: The big fan at the front of an airliner engine is also turned by the turbine at the back (added in O-010. Sources: ASME Landmark #135 "Neuchâtel Gas Turbine", JSME "Mechanical Engineering Heritage No.007")

4-30.name: Three-phase AC transmission
4-30.hee1: Power lines on utility poles come in sets of three because they carry three-phase AC. (Added in O-011. Sources: IEEE Milestones "Rotating Fields and Early Induction Motors", Wikipedia "Mikhail Dolivo-Dobrovolsky")

4-31.name: Nuclear power
4-31.hee1: The first nuclear power lit up four light bulbs ⚠️ (Added in O-011. Sources: ASME Landmark #39 "EBR-I", ASME Landmark #47 "Shippingport", Wikipedia "Nuclear power")

4-32.name: High-voltage direct current transmission
4-32.hee1: When sending electricity far through cables on the sea floor, direct current wastes less than alternating current. (Added in O-011. Sources: IEEE Milestones "Gotland High Voltage Direct Current Link, 1954", ETHW "Uno Lamm")

4-33.name: Water turbine
4-33.hee1: The wheel in a hydroelectric plant is not an old wooden water wheel but a turbine with metal blades (added in O-011. Sources: ASME Landmark #57 "Kaplan Turbine", #157 "Pelton Waterwheel", Wikipedia "Water turbine")

5-01.name: Hand piston pump
5-01.hee1: Because of the weight of air, even horses cannot pull them apart.

5-02.name: Vacuum tube
5-02.hee1: Before transistors, signals were amplified with parts that looked like glass light bulbs.

5-03.name: Mercury column and pressure units
5-03.hee1: The "hPa (hectopascal)" in weather forecasts is named after Pascal.

5-04.name: Rotary vane oil pump
5-04.hee1: The "hummm" sound in a lab is this pump

5-05.name: Mercury diffusion pump
5-05.hee1: It has no moving parts, yet blows air away with a wind of vapor.

5-06.name: Oil diffusion pump
5-06.hee1: Instead of mercury, it uses a special oil that hardly evaporates.

5-07.name: Turbomolecular pump
5-07.hee1: The tips of its blades spin at nearly the speed of sound.

5-08.name: Ion pump
5-08.hee1: Instead of pushing air out, it traps it inside metal

5-09.name: Cryopump → liquid nitrogen cold trap
5-09.hee1: It freezes the air and sticks it to the wall.

5-10.name: Vacuum gauge
5-10.hee1: It measures the "emptiness" of empty space by how fast a wire cools down.

5-11.name: Vacuum chamber
5-11.hee1: Gas seeps out even from the metal walls, so they are baked to drive it out.

5-12.name: Vacuum seal
5-12.hee1: The wires at the base of a light bulb are a special metal that expands and shrinks just as much as glass

5-14.name: Vacuum deposition
5-14.hee1: The silver inside a potato chip bag is also aluminum from vacuum deposition.

5-15.name: Sprengel mercury pump
5-15.hee1: The vacuum in light bulbs was made with drops of mercury.

5-16.name: Getter
5-16.hee1: The silver part of a vacuum tube is the mark left after it ate up the leftover air.

6-02.name: Gas holder
6-02.hee1: 1) Gas tanks in the gas-lamp era used water as their lid 2) The pressure is the bell's weight ÷ its area 3) At King's Cross in London, the frames remain, now part of parks and homes 4) Hydrogen escapes even through gaps in metal

6-03.name: Compressor
6-03.hee1: In the 1880s high-pressure cylinders appeared, and gases could be carried around.

6-04.name: Rock salt mine
6-04.hee1: Rock salt is "a sea that turned to stone".

6-05.name: Chlor-alkali electrolysis
6-05.hee1: Salt gives chlorine and caustic soda at the same time

6-06.name: Hydrochloric acid
6-06.hee1: Burn hydrogen in chlorine and you get hydrogen chloride; dissolve it in water and you get hydrochloric acid.

6-07.name: Air separation
6-07.hee1: Turn air into a liquid and "distill" it.

6-08.name: Noble gas purification
6-08.hee1: Most of the gas in an excimer laser is neon.

6-09.name: Haber-Bosch process
6-09.hee1: The catalyst is made from magnetite

6-11.name: Nitric acid
6-11.hee1: Pour sulfuric acid on saltpeter and nitric acid comes out.

6-12.name: Lead chamber process sulfuric acid
6-12.hee1: Why sulfuric acid factories were made of lead.

6-13.name: Contact process sulfuric acid
6-13.hee1: With a catalyst such as platinum, you can make very strong sulfuric acid

6-14.name: Fluorine gas
6-14.hee1: Fluorine is the "most dangerous element": several chemists were poisoned before it was isolated.

6-15.name: Helium (avoided)
6-15.hee1: Helium was found on the Sun first (spectroscopy of the 1868 eclipse). On Earth we can only get the helium that built up underground from radioactive decay.

6-16.name: Collecting natural saltpeter
6-16.hee1: An ingredient for gunpowder was taken from the soil of old animal sheds.

7-01.name: Optical glass
7-01.hee1: Adding lead makes glass sparkle (crystal glass)

7-02.name: Fused quartz
7-02.hee1: Burn hydrogen and oxygen together, and it gets hot enough to melt quartz.

7-03.name: Lens grinding
7-03.hee1: Lenses are polished not with hard tools, but with soft pitch.

7-04.name: Refracting telescope and achromatic lens
7-04.hee1: Gluing two kinds of glass together removes the rainbow-colored blur.

7-05.name: Reflecting mirror
7-05.hee1: Silver mirrors are made by a chemical reaction that coats glass with silver from a solution

7-06.name: Prism spectroscopy
7-06.hee1: Split light into a rainbow, and you can tell what stars are made of.

7-07.name: Diffraction grating
7-07.hee1: The rainbow colors on the back of a CD come from a diffraction grating too.

7-09.name: Interferometer
7-09.hee1: If you use light waves as a ruler, you can measure one hundredth of a hair.

7-10.name: Mercury lamp
7-10.hee1: Semiconductor factories use yellow light because it is a color the resist does not react to

7-11.name: Silver halide photomask
7-11.hee1: The circuit patterns of the first ICs were made by cutting film by hand.

7-12.name: Chrome mask
7-12.hee1: The "master copy" of a circuit is a shadow picture made of thin metal on clear quartz.

7-13.name: Laser principle
7-13.hee1: The first laser shone using a ruby gemstone.

7-14.name: CO2 laser
7-14.hee1: This laser's light can't pass through glass, so its windows are salt crystals

7-15.name: Ultraviolet optical materials
7-15.hee1: Natural fluorite becomes the window of cutting-edge lasers.

7-16.name: Immersion optics
7-16.hee1: Just putting water between the lens and the wafer lets you draw finer patterns.

7-17.name: Multilayer mirror
7-17.hee1: Light that one layer cannot reflect is bounced back by stacking 40 weak reflections.

7-18.name: EUV light source
7-18.hee1: Falling droplets of tin are hit by a laser to make them glow

7-19.name: Projection lens
7-19.hee1: The lens of a lithography machine is a "tower of glass" stacking dozens of lenses.

7-20.name: Excimer laser
7-20.hee1: "Excimer" means "a pair that sticks together only when excited."

7-21.name: Ultra-low expansion glass
7-21.hee1: Glass whose length hardly changes whether you heat it or cool it.

7-22.name: Anti-reflection coating
7-22.hee1: Stack thin films on glass and the glass becomes "invisible" (added in IMP-24, network_proposals W-3)

7-23.name: LiDAR
7-23.hee1: Apollo 15 measured the bumps of the Moon by timing how long laser light took to bounce back from its surface. (Added in S-005. Sources: Wikipedia "Lidar", Frontiers in Remote Sensing (2022) "LiDAR history")

7-24.name: Camera autofocus
7-24.hee1: The first mass-produced camera that focuses by itself was made by Konica of Japan, in 1977. (Added in S-004. Sources: en.wikipedia.org, en.wikipedia.org, en.wikipedia.org, Camera-wiki "Konica C35 AF", Fstoppers "Autofocus Turns 50" (https://camera-wiki.org/wiki/Konica_C35_AF))

7-25.name: Semiconductor laser
7-25.hee1: The light running through optical fibers comes from semiconductor lasers smaller than a grain of rice. (Added in O-010. Sources: IEEE Milestones "Semiconductor Laser, 1962", Wikipedia "Laser diode")

7-26.name: Holography
7-26.hee1: The shiny patterns on banknotes and cards are holograms that record a whole light wave (added in O-011. Sources: IEEE Milestones "Invention of Holography, 1947", Wikipedia "Holography")

8-01.name: Lathe
8-01.hee1: A lathe that moves the cutter with a lead screw removed the shaking of human hands.

8-02.name: Screw cutting and interchangeable parts
8-02.hee1: Screws from any shop fit because the angle of the thread is standardized.

8-03.name: Flat surfaces and surface plates
8-03.hee1: The way to make "perfectly flat" from nothing is to rub three plates against each other.

8-04.name: Calipers and micrometers
8-04.hee1: If you know how many mm a screw moves in one turn, you can measure 0.01 mm

8-05.name: Gauge block
8-05.hee1: Metal pieces that are flat enough stick together without glue.

8-06.name: Interferometric length measurement
8-06.hee1: The definition of one meter changed from a metal bar to light.

8-07.name: Vibration isolation and constant temperature
8-07.hee1: In a precision factory, work stops just because a truck drives by.

8-08.name: Ball-screw precision stage
8-08.hee1: Little steel balls roll inside the screw's groove

8-09.name: Linear motor and air bearing stage
8-09.hee1: The stage of a lithography machine accelerates like a roller coaster and stops to the nanometer.

8-10.name: Optical microscope
8-10.hee1: With a light microscope, you cannot see things smaller than the wavelength of light.

8-11.name: Electron microscope
8-11.hee1: Using electrons instead of "light" lets you see even viruses.

8-12.name: Ruling engine
8-12.hee1: If the temperature changed during the many days of ruling, the work failed

8-13.name: Droplet generator
8-13.hee1: EUV light sources and inkjet printers are relatives.

8-14.name: Precision lens barrel assembly
8-14.hee1: Even the best lens blurs if it is assembled 0.001 mm off.

8-15.name: Quartz crystal oscillator
8-15.hee1: Inside a wristwatch, a quartz crystal vibrates 32,768 times a second.

8-16.name: Scanning probe microscope
8-16.hee1: It sees the bumps of single atoms by tracing them with a sharp needle

8-17.name: Alignment
8-17.hee1: Dozens of transparent pictures are stacked off by only a few ten-thousandths of a hair's width.

8-18.name: Synthetic quartz
8-18.hee1: Almost all the quartz in watches is artificial crystal grown in a pressure cooker.

8-19.name: Pulley
8-19.hee1: You need only a quarter of the force, but you pull the rope four times as far. (Added in IMP-24, network_proposals N-1)

8-20.name: Ball bearing
8-20.hee1: Put steel balls in between, and things roll instead of rubbing. That is why wheels and motors turn easily (added in NET-06. Sources: Wikipedia "Bearing (mechanical)", Schaeffler "Impeccably round and smooth", Wikipedia "Jules Suriray", Wikipedia "Sven Gustaf Wingqvist")

8-21.name: Sextant
8-21.hee1: Line up the Sun with the horizon using two mirrors, and you can tell where on Earth you are. (Added in NET-06. Sources: Wikipedia "Sextant", "Octant (instrument)", Grace's Guide "John Hadley")

8-22.name: Meter prototype
8-22.hee1: One meter was a length decided from the size of the Earth. (Added in NET-06. Sources: Wikipedia "Mètre des Archives", Quality Magazine "The Emergence of the Metric System")

8-23.name: International Prototype of the Kilogram
8-23.hee1: Until 2019, one kilogram was the weight of a single lump of metal in a vault in Paris. (Added in NET-06. Sources: Wikipedia "International Prototype of the Kilogram", EPFL Graph Search)

8-24.name: International System of Units (SI)
8-24.hee1: The whole world can use the same "1 meter" and "1 second" thanks to the SI, decided in 1960 (added in NET-06. Source: BIPM "Resolution 12 of the 11th CGPM (1960)")

8-25.name: Watt balance
8-25.hee1: Today one kilogram is defined not by a lump of metal but by electric force. (Added in NET-06. Sources: NPL "Bryan Kibble", NIST "Kilogram: Kibble balance", Comptes Rendus Physique 2019)

8-26.name: Typewriter
8-26.hee1: The key layout on computers is the same layout typewriters used 150 years ago. (Added in S-002. Sources: Wikipedia "QWERTY", Computer Hope "Why is the keyboard not in alphabetical order")

8-27.name: Strain wave gearing
8-27.hee1: Inside a robot's joints, a metal gear ring turns while bending into a wobbly oval. (Added in S-005. Sources: Wikipedia "Strain wave gearing", "Walton Musser", Harmonic Drive LLC 'C. Walton Musser' (announced 1957, US Patent 2,906,143) (https://legacy.harmonicdrive.net/aboutus/musser/))

8-28.name: Strain gauge
8-28.hee1: The strain gauge was thought up by a researcher studying how water tanks shake in earthquakes (added in S-005. Sources: Caltech "Engineering and Science: Simmons", Micro-Measurements "Strain gage history")

8-29.name: Roller chain
8-29.hee1: The shape of a bicycle chain has barely changed from the design thought up more than 140 years ago. (Added in S-004. Sources: en.wikipedia.org, gracesguide.co.uk)

8-30.name: Atomic clock
8-30.hee1: Today one second is defined as the time it takes a cesium atom to vibrate 9,192,631,770 times. (Added in O-006. Sources: IEEE Milestones "First Atomic Clock, 1948", NIST, Wikipedia "Atomic clock")

8-31.name: Grinding machine
8-31.hee1: Even steel too hard to cut with a blade can be shaped to one hundredth of a hair's accuracy by rubbing it with a grinding wheel. (Added in O-009. Sources: JSME "Mechanical Engineering Heritage No.059, No.114, No.106", Wikipedia "Grinding machine", Schaeffler "Impeccably round and smooth")

8-32.name: Gear cutting machine
8-32.hee1: Accuracy rose by remaking the gears of the gear-making machine more precisely, again and again (added in O-010. Sources: JSME "Mechanical Engineering Heritage No.034", Wikipedia "Hobbing")

8-33.name: Mass spectrometry
8-33.hee1: When bent by an electromagnet, atoms fly apart sorted by weight. (Added in O-010. Sources: Nobel Prize "Chemistry 1922", "Chemistry 2002", Wikipedia "National Historic Chemical Landmarks")

8-34.name: NC
8-34.hee1: The first NC machine tool moved its cutter by reading paper tape with holes punched in it. (Added in O-010. Sources: JSME "Mechanical Engineering Heritage No.126", Wikipedia "Numerical control" "John T. Parsons")

8-35.name: Quartz wristwatch
8-35.hee1: The quartz crystal in a quartz watch vibrates as many as 32,768 times a second. (Added in O-010. Sources: JSME "Mechanical Engineering Heritage No.066", Wikipedia "Seiko Astron")

8-36.name: Tilting-pad thrust bearing
8-36.hee1: The hundreds of tons of a big water turbine are held up floating on just a thin film of oil (added in O-011. Sources: ASME Landmark #123 "Kingsbury Thrust Bearing", Wikipedia "Fluid bearing")

8-37.name: Electrical discharge machining
8-37.hee1: Tens of thousands of sparks per second melt and carve hard metal bit by bit. (Added in O-011. Sources: Wikipedia "Electrical discharge machining", National Museum of Nature and Science "Essential Historical Materials for Science and Technology")

8-38.name: Cryo-electron microscope
8-38.hee1: If water is frozen in an instant, no ice crystals form and it sets solid like glass. (Added in O-011. Sources: Nobel Prize "Chemistry 2017", Nobel Prize "Chemistry 2017 press release" (https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2017/press-release/))

8-39.name: Arc welding
8-39.hee1: The light from arc welding is so strong that welders protect their eyes with a dark mask. (Added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Arc welding", ASME Landmark #44)

8-40.name: Gas welding and cutting
8-40.hee1: An oxygen-acetylene flame is about 3100°C and cuts iron like butter ⚠️ (added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Oxy-fuel welding and cutting", "Edmond Fouché", Linde "A Look at The History of Welding" (https://www.lindedirect.com/blogs/industrial-guides/industrial-guides/2024/01/30/a-look-at-the-history-of-welding))

8-41.name: Hydraulic forging press
8-41.hee1: A 50,000-ton press is as big as a building several stories tall ⚠️ (Added in O-012. Sources: Wikipedia "Heavy Press Program", ASME Landmark #71 and #89)

8-42.name: Dividing engine
8-42.hee1: Sextant scales came to be engraved by a machine instead of by hand. (Added in O-012. Sources: Smithsonian NMAH 694508, MacTutor "Jesse Ramsden", Wikipedia "Dividing engine")

9-01.name: Ge zone refining
9-01.hee1: Passing a molten band through many times gathers the impurities at one end.

9-02.name: Zone leveling
9-02.hee1: Moving the molten zone back and forth spreads the added impurity evenly through the whole bar

9-03.name: Point-contact transistor
9-03.hee1: Two gold contacts were pressed onto germanium with a plastic wedge.

9-04.name: Alloy-junction transistor
9-04.hee1: Put a bead of indium on each side of germanium and bake it, and you get a three-layer part.

9-05.name: Ge diode
9-05.hee1: A part with a thin needle standing on germanium caught radar waves.

9-06.name: Oxide etching
9-06.hee1: When the oxide is fully dissolved, the surface repels water (hydrophobic), so you can see with your eyes when it's done

9-07.name: Ge single-crystal pulling
9-07.hee1: Inside the company, people objected: "We don't need single crystals."

9-08.name: CZ process
9-08.hee1: Most of the world's silicon is made with a method born from an accident 100 years ago.

9-09.name: Float-zone (FZ) method
9-09.hee1: With no crucible, liquid silicon is held up by surface tension alone.

9-10.name: Grown-junction transistor
9-10.hee1: Materials were mixed in while the crystal was growing, making 3 layers inside

9-11.name: Dopant sources
9-11.hee1: Arsenic is poison, but it is also in the transistors inside your smartphone.

9-12.name: Wafer slicing
9-12.hee1: When wafers are sliced, a large part turns into dust and is lost.

9-13.name: Lapping and mirror polishing
9-13.hee1: The bumps on a mirror-polished wafer are only a few dozen atoms high.

9-14.name: RCA clean
9-14.hee1: A recipe from more than 50 years ago is still the basis in today's most advanced factories

9-15.name: Thermal oxidation
9-15.hee1: Silicon's own "rust" turns into glass and protects it.

9-16.name: Thermal diffusion
9-16.hee1: Bake at 1000°C for hours, and atoms walk little by little through the solid.

9-17.name: Mesa transistor
9-17.hee1: "Mesa" means table in Spanish. It is the shape of the flat-topped hills in the American West.

9-18.name: Planar process
9-18.hee1: The idea of "making it while keeping it flat" was the start of the IC

9-19.name: Resist coating
9-19.hee1: It's just like spinning pizza dough to spread it out.

9-20.name: Contact and proximity printing
9-20.hee1: The first ICs were made by printing the shadow of a mask, like a shadow picture.

9-21.name: Development and post-bake
9-21.hee1: The circuit is brought out with the same steps as developing a photograph.

9-22.name: Integrated circuit
9-22.hee1: The first IC was one transistor and a few parts, about the size of a fingertip

9-23.name: MOSFET
9-23.hee1: Of all the things humans have ever made, the MOSFET is the most numerous.

9-24.name: CMOS
9-24.hee1: Calculator and watch batteries last for years thanks to CMOS.

9-25.name: Metal wiring
9-25.hee1: The wires inside a chip are the same metal as aluminum foil.

9-27.name: Dry etching
9-27.hee1: Dissolving with liquid also eats sideways, so an electric discharge is used to carve straight down only.

9-28.name: Ion implantation
9-28.hee1: Atoms are used as bullets and shot to an exact depth.

9-29.name: Annealing
9-29.hee1: Just like annealing metal, heat lets the atoms line up again.

9-30.name: Epitaxy and CVD
9-30.hee1: The reaction that thickens rods in the Siemens process is used to make thin films

9-31.name: CMP (chemical mechanical polishing)
9-31.hee1: Like building a skyscraper of dozens of floors, flattening each floor one at a time.

9-32.name: Dicing
9-32.hee1: Hundreds of chips are cut out of a single wafer.

9-33.name: Wire bonding
9-33.hee1: The wire connecting the chip to the outside is gold about a third as thick as a hair.

9-34.name: Encapsulation
9-34.hee1: The outside of a black chip is plastic, like a shell protecting it from moisture

9-35.name: Testing
9-35.hee1: Not every chip that is made actually works.

9-36.name: Copper interconnects
9-36.hee1: The name of Damascus inlay work is used for the most advanced wiring.

9-37.name: FinFET
9-37.hee1: The transistor went from a one-story house to a "standing plate".

9-38.name: GAA (gate-all-around)
9-38.hee1: In the end, the gate wraps all the way around the channel

9-39.name: Reduction projection lithography
9-39.hee1: The history of semiconductors is the history of "shorter light, finer patterns".

9-40.name: EUV lithography machine
9-40.hee1: A "camera" bigger than a house that only one company in the world can make.

9-41.name: Power semiconductors and inverters
9-41.hee1: An electric car turns electricity on and off thousands of times a second to drive its motor. (Added in IMP-24, network_proposals N-4, N-5)

9-42.name: Image sensor
9-42.hee1: Phone cameras and optical mice both use the same family of chips that "turn light into electrons and count them" (added in S-003. Sources: Nobel Prize "Physics 2009", Wikipedia "Active-pixel sensor", "Optical mouse")

9-43.name: MEMS
9-43.hee1: Inside a smartphone are tiny springs and weights made of silicon, and they really move when you tilt it. (Added in S-003. Sources: Proc. IEEE "Silicon as a Mechanical Material" (1982), Wikipedia "Microelectromechanical systems")

9-44.name: Thermistor
9-44.hee1: An air conditioner's thermometer is a tiny ceramic bead that lets electricity flow more easily as it warms up. (Added in S-004. Sources: shura.shu.ac.uk, murata.com)

9-45.name: Bayer filter
9-45.hee1: Half of a camera's pixels are green, because the human eye is most sensitive to green. (Added in S-004. Sources: patents.google.com, en.wikipedia.org)

9-46.name: Sensors that detect people
9-46.hee1: Motion sensors don't sense "a human shape" but "changes" in the infrared from your body, so the light may go off if you stay still. (added in S-004. Sources: logosfoundation.org, en.wikipedia.org)

9-47.name: Particle accelerator
9-47.hee1: Semiconductor factories have rows of small accelerators (ion implanters). (Added in O-008. Sources: Nobel Prize "Physics 1939", "Physics 1951", University of Bern "Greinacher", DESY "Wideröe")

9-48.name: Semiconductor heterostructure
9-48.hee1: The lasers in CDs and optical fibers shine inside a sandwich of different semiconductors stacked atoms thick. (Added in O-009. Sources: Nobel Prize "Physics 2000", Kyoto Prize, IEEE Milestones "HEMT 1979", Semiconductor History Museum of Japan (SSIS))

9-49.name: Thyristor
9-49.hee1: The devices that change the speed of train motors were first made with semiconductor switches called thyristors. (Added in O-011. Sources: IEEE Milestones "SCR/Thyristor, 1957", ETHW IEEE Milestones 'SCR/Thyristor, 1957' / IEEE Spectrum (https://ethw.org/Milestones:SCR/Thyristor,_1957))

B-01.name: Incandescent light bulb
B-01.hee1: The vacuum tube was born from adding one metal plate inside a light bulb.

B-02.name: Silver halide photography
B-02.hee1: The ancestor of photolithography (a setup for Chapter 3, [7-11]).

B-02a.name: Daguerreotype
B-02a.hee1: Each picture is one of a kind and cannot be copied (there is no negative).

B-02b.name: Wet plate photography → gelatin dry plate
B-02b.hee1: Many prints from one glass negative = the photolithography idea of copying many times from one mask

B-03.name: X-ray tube
B-03.hee1: X-rays were named X because they were "rays of unknown nature".

B-04.name: Magnetron and microwave oven
B-04.hee1: The microwave oven was born from a radar part.

B-05.name: Polarization
B-05.hee1: Put a clear calcite crystal on some writing and the letters look doubled. (Moved from [7-08])

B-06.name: Polarizing film
B-06.hee1: In front of an LCD screen is a film dyed with iodine

B-07.name: LED
B-07.hee1: Only after the blue LED was made could white LEDs finally be made.

B-08.name: Electronic calculator
B-08.hee1: The first calculator weighed as much as a whole desk.

B-09.name: Game console
B-09.hee1: The Famicom's CPU is a grandchild of the technology that gave birth to the calculator.

B-10.name: Smartphone
B-10.hee1: In your pocket, millions of times the computing power of the Apollo computer

B-11.name: AI chip
B-11.hee1: Starting from stone tools, you reach the parts of a thinking machine.

B-12.name: Solar cell
B-12.hee1: A solar cell uses the same p-n junction as a transistor.

B-13.name: Mauveine
B-13.hee1: The chemical industry began from a failed experiment to make a medicine.

B-14.name: Acetylene lamp
B-14.hee1: A stone that gives off a burnable gas when you drip water on it

B-15.name: Tofu
B-15.hee1: From nigari, which sets tofu, you can get magnesium metal ([1-39]).

B-16.name: Personal computer
B-16.hee1: Computers that sit on a desk all went on sale at once in 1977.

B-17.name: GPS
B-17.hee1: From the time differences of signals sent by satellites in the sky, you can tell where you are.

B-18.name: Liquid crystal display
B-18.hee1: Liquid crystal doesn't glow by itself; electricity turns it to open and close the path for light (added in S-002. Sources: Wikipedia "Liquid crystal", "Twisted nematic field effect", KIT "100 Objekte")

B-19.name: TFT LCD
B-19.hee1: Behind each pixel of a screen is one thin transistor, and millions of them are lined up on glass. (Added in S-002. Sources: Wikipedia "Thin-film transistor", IEEE Milestones "Amorphous Silicon TFT Switches")

B-20.name: White LED backlight
B-20.hee1: A white LED is really a blue LED covered with a powder that glows yellow; blue and yellow mix to look white. (Added in S-002. Sources: Semiconductor History Museum of Japan (SSIS) "White LED", LEDinside)

B-21.name: Ball mouse
B-21.hee1: The first mouse was a wooden box with two wheels, not a ball. (Added in S-002. Sources: Computer History Museum "Revolution: Input & Output", Wikipedia "Bill English")

B-22.name: Optical mouse
B-22.hee1: An optical mouse takes more than 1000 pictures of the desk surface per second and works out motion from how the pattern shifts (added in S-002. Sources: Wikipedia "Optical mouse", "IntelliMouse")

B-23.name: Dissolved acetylene and the automatic lighthouse flasher
B-23.hee1: Old lighthouses had a device that sensed daylight and put out the flame automatically during the day. (Added in O-008. Sources: Nobel Prize "Physics 1912 Award Ceremony Speech", Wikipedia "Agamassan", Linda Hall Library "Gustaf Dalén")

I-01.name: Electromagnetic induction
I-01.hee1: Electricity flows only while you are moving a magnet inside a coil. Stop, and it stops.

I-02.name: Thermodynamics
I-02.hee1: An engine's power depends not on "how hot" but on "the difference between the hot side and the cold side"

I-03.name: Periodic table
I-03.hee1: Mendeleev predicted the weight and properties of germanium before it was discovered.

I-04.name: Resolution limit of light
